title: From Michelangelo to 'the eye or chemistry?'
summary: A buried Cupid sold as an antique, and the 1920s trial that set the expert's eye against the chemist.

shots.title:
Faking is
as old as art.
shots.subtitle: Even Michelangelo's work was sold as an **antique**.
shots.narration: Forgery is not a modern crime. Our first case involves the most famous sculptor of the Renaissance, and comes from the first great biographer of artists.

shots.text: A life-size **sleeping Cupid**, carved by Michelangelo in Florence.
shots.narration: Giorgio Vasari tells how Michelangelo carved a life-size sleeping Cupid in Florence — and how a patron suggested a profitable deception.

shots.text: If you were to bury it under ground and then sent it to Rome treated in such a manner as to make it look old, I am certain that it would pass for an antique, and you would thus obtain much more for it than by selling it here.
shots.by: Lorenzo di Pier Francesco de' Medici, as reported by Vasari (trans. G. de Vere)
shots.narration: The advice, as Vasari reports it: bury it, make it look old, send it to Rome, and it will pass for an antique — and fetch far more.

shots.text: Sold to a cardinal as an antique — for **200 ducats**.
shots.narration: In one of Vasari's versions, a dealer sold it to Cardinal San Giorgio as an antique for two hundred ducats, and told Michelangelo it had fetched only thirty crowns.

shots.text: The cardinal found out — and **got his money back**.
shots.narration: When the cardinal learned it had been made in Florence, he forced the dealer's agent to return the money. Lesson one: the story told about an object is part of the fake.

shots.text: c. 1923: a 'Frans Hals' **Laughing Cavalier**, published by the leading expert.
shots.narration: Fast-forward to the 1920s. Cornelis Hofstede de Groot, a leading expert on Dutch painting, accepted a small 'Laughing Cavalier' as a Frans Hals and published it in The Burlington Magazine.

shots.heading: What the court's experts reported
shots.narration: When the buyer sued, the experts reported modern materials: zinc white, cobalt blue, artificial ultramarine, and machine-made nails in an X-ray. It was the first time such evidence exposed a fake in a Dutch court.

shots.text: Real or fake? **The eye or chemistry?**
shots.footnote: C. Hofstede de Groot, Echt of onecht? Oog of chemie?, 1925
shots.narration: Hofstede de Groot would not back down. He bought the painting to end the case, and published a book whose title says it all: Real or fake? The eye or chemistry?

shots.text: Another 'Hals' he bought turned out to contain **water-soluble paint**.
shots.narration: He did it twice. Another 'Hals' he bought in 1923 was declared a forgery because its paint dissolved in water. He defended both to the end.

shots.text: The Laughing Cavalier is **back under examination**.
shots.narration: The Laughing Cavalier resurfaced in 2024, and a European research project on forgery detection is now re-examining it, with the court archive in hand. Its findings are not yet peer reviewed.

steps.title: Eye, lab or archive?
steps.brief: Every piece of evidence about a painting comes from one of three places. Sort these into the expert's eye, the laboratory, or the documents.

cards.text: The modelling of the face feels too timid for the master.
cards.why: A stylistic judgement — the connoisseur's domain.

cards.text: An expert's published certificate of authenticity.
cards.why: A certificate records an opinion; it adds no new physical evidence.

cards.text: Zinc white in the original paint layer.
cards.why: Material evidence: zinc white became available to artists only in the early 19th century.

cards.text: Machine-made nails visible in an X-radiograph.
cards.why: Metal shows up in X-rays, and machine-made nails date the construction.

cards.text: A dealer's story that the work comes from an old family collection.
cards.why: A provenance claim — to be checked against documents.

cards.text: A sale catalogue from 1850 giving the picture's subject and size.
cards.why: A document that can tie the object to a past owner.

questions.prompt: According to Vasari, how was Michelangelo's Cupid to pass as ancient?
options: It was signed with a Greek name
It was buried and treated to look old
questions.explain: Lorenzo di Pier Francesco suggested burying it and making it look old before sending it to Rome.

questions.prompt: Which findings did the court's experts report in the Laughing Cavalier?
questions.explain: Modern pigments and machine-made nails; the ultramarine reported was the artificial kind.

questions.prompt: What was Hofstede de Groot's position?
options: His expert eye should outweigh the chemical evidence
questions.explain: His book's title sums it up: Real or fake? The eye or chemistry?
